articles.title: THE ASSEMBLY IN EVERY PLACE
articles.author: G. W. Brown
articles.place: Word in meeting for ministry, Plainfield, N.J.

paragraphs.text: This occasion is in a local setting, nevertheless the Spirit of God might use anyone at this time or at any such time. He knows what we need, whereas one visiting may not know. What is pressing upon one at this time is the truth concerning the assembly as anticipated by the Lord in the first verse we read. It is a position which is surely open to us now. When the Lord spoke these words the Holy Spirit had not come. In the sense in which He was speaking, I suppose, there would not be “two or three … gathered together unto my name”; but the Spirit having come, this became possible and it is possible up to the present moment. “Where two or three are gathered together unto my name, there am I in the midst of them”. I wonder, dear brethren, if we are in faith as to that. We would desire to be in such a company, but whether we are in faith as to the presence of the Lord and His power, or whether in the secret of our souls we acknowledge His presence, would be a test to us. “There am I in the midst of them”. In one sense that would be anticipative, the Spirit then not having come.

But when we come to Paul’s word to the Corinthians, the Spirit had come. He says, “The assembly of God which is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called saints”, that is, saints by divine calling in that city. And what he is about

to say to saints in that city would apply to saints in every place in such a setting—“with all that in every place call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both theirs and ours”. Now you have the fulfilment of that of which the Lord spoke anticipatively, “there am I in the midst of them”. It is a most blessed privilege if we can rise to it, and if we have faith to realise it. Now, the Spirit having come, the apostle can refer to “the assembly of God which is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus ... with all that in every place” (that is, in a similar setting in other places) “call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both theirs and ours”. What respect becomes us, dear brethren, for every such setting, wherever it may be! “There am I in the midst of them”. It is the assembly of God. Corinth is gone, and the well-defined position in that city does not exist today. But surely what follows provides for our own time—“all that in every place call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both theirs and ours”. Now I say, dear brethren, what respect becomes us as we contemplate the saints in every city.

When we come to Acts, we see what respect Paul had. It says, “And having gone up and saluted the assembly, he went down to Antioch”. I think that implies, as do similar references to “having saluted the brethren” and “having saluted them” (Acts 21: 7, 19), the respect Paul would have for the assembly in each place.

I do not feel that more need be said, except that one prays for oneself and for one’s brethren that we might be kept and maintained in a holy respect for the saints in such settings, as Paul anticipated.

articles.title: NO CONDEMNATION TO THOSE IN CHRIST JESUS
articles.author: A. B. Parker
articles.place: Word at meeting for ministry, Plainfield, N.J.

paragraphs.text: Numbers 23: 4 (“God met Balaam”); 23: 16 (“Jehovah met Balaam”); 24: 2 (“The Spirit of God came upon him”); Romans 8: 1, 2, 26, 31–The great matter of God being for us is in mind—“If God be for us, who against us?”. I believe that the type, of which we have read, would show that God, known as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, is for us. This would be implied by the use of the three different titles used for God in the passages read in Numbers. So we can say, according to Romans, that the Father is for us, the Son is for us, and the Holy Spirit is for us. God spared not His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all—Christ has died for us; “who is also at the right hand of God; who also intercedes for us”; the Spirit joins its help to our weakness and makes intercession for us. To understand that each divine Person is for us is a very great matter. The passage indicates that They are for those who are “in Christ Jesus”. This is very wonderful, but it is also very challenging. “There is then now no condemnation to those in Christ Jesus”. How much do I understand and experience what it is to be in Christ Jesus? If I am to appropriate the great fact of God being for me, I must not overlook the fact that this applies to those who are “in Christ Jesus”. It may be said that that passage is abstract, and surely it is, but I believe that it is to be experienced in a concrete way.

If it were not for the “in Christ Jesus” position, the breakdown of the church would have been the end of the testimony, but in 2 Timothy Paul shows us that in spite of public breakdown “the firm foundation of God stands”. It is because everything that has been despoiled by man’s failure is safely preserved in Christ Jesus. The expression “in Christ Jesus” is used time and again in 2 Timothy, lifting our hearts to an area where there is no breakdown; where everything is continuing intact. Publicly there is scattering and breakdown so that it is impossible to identify the church, as such, (thank God, we can identify features of it). But in the sphere which is designated “in Christ Jesus”, there is no confusion; all is clearly defined—the shewbread is on the pure table. When the government of God came upon Israel because of Solomon’s breakdown and Rehoboam’s weakness, the kingdom was divided. Ten tribes were given to Jeroboam and two remained with Rehoboam, but in the temple, which was in Judah, the service of God continued and the twelve loaves on the pure table were maintained as before. Before God there is no division; everything there is according to purpose; all Israel shall be saved (Romans 11: 26).

The parables which Balaam was required to utter should be of great encouragement to us. We know from Israel’s history that there was much breakdown and failure in the wilderness. Moses was greatly tried, but there was always the means, in God’s hand, to bridge the gap of Israel’s failure, whether it was the manna, or the golden censer, or the rod of Aaron that budded—all spoke of Christ, typically, as maintaining the people. Then, finally, the brazen serpent and the springing well—all serving to bring about in Israel a state in keeping with what was

kept inviolate in the divine presence. The pattern to which the people were being held was in what was before God, in the candlestick and the shewbread on the pure table. And so it is at the present time, as we have been saying; in the midst of great confusion we can resort to a realm “in Christ Jesus” where all is held in perfect order, where the soul of the believer can find its resort. To do so is to experience why there is no condemnation.

It is a wonderful thing to consider that the vast majority of those who form the assembly are now safely housed with Christ in His sphere. The time of testimony is nearly over. What triumph there is in knowing that the vast majority—those who have departed to be with Christ—are now absolutely subject to Christ’s lordship. For them there is no more strife, no envying, no division of thought. “Christ has died and lived again, that he might rule over both dead and living”, Romans 14: 9. His lordship is fully recognised, already, by the vast majority of the saints. The trouble is down here. How it would stimulate us to resort to the “in Christ Jesus” sphere where all is in perfect order in the mind of God and in the heart of Christ, and to realise that all will soon be established, publicly, according to what is there. In the meantime, “Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect? It is God who justifies— who is he that condemns?” But, notice, it is “God’s elect”—those whom He regards in relation to His purpose, whom He is forming to conform to His purpose, and it is in that light that He regards us when Balaam would curse.

Of course, there is the side of our responsibility, and the enemy would seek to overwhelm us, so that in a practical way we need to learn how God is for us, to help us in our time of need. We are told that God spared not His on Son, but delivered Him up for us all, and we are assured that with Him He will grant us all things. We need not lack anything; God will give us all that we need. As knowing Him we are free to spread our needs before Him and He will supply, according to His will, what we have need of.

As to Christ being for us, we are told that He has died for us, but, great as that is, He now lives for us; He ever appears in the presence of God for us. When He faced death He said, “This is my body which is given for you”, Luke 22: 19. In the glory, He told Paul, “This is my body which is for you”, 1 Corinthians 11: 24. How fully He is for us!

The Holy Spirit has come—another Comforter—to bring us through all the trials and temptations in view of our soon being conformed to Christ’s likeness. On the way, we may become discouraged; circumstances tend to overwhelm us; we do not know what to pray for as we ought; we may cease to pray. It is then that the Spirit takes over; He joins His help to our weakness; He makes intercession for us with groanings that cannot be uttered. Our feelings, sorrowful as they may be, are surpassed by the feelings of the blessed Spirit, who takes our matters on and represents our cause before God, who searches our hearts and knows the mind of the Spirit. What is that mind? Life and peace (Romans 8: 6). God, in searching our hearts, finds a moral basis for bringing in relief. And how does he bring in that relief? By bringing us, in our spirits, into the “in Christ Jesus” position. We begin to see how God has been for us, even in a past eternity, but how He is now for us, for “whom he has predestinated, these also he has called; and whom he has called, these also he has justified; but whom he has justified, these also he has glorified”. What relief! What joy to be transferred from deep distress to present glory! Thus God is for us in the Spirit. God is for us—Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Let us glory in this fact that God is for us.

Well, dear brethren, may we not then be encouraged to learn more about this wonderful realm “in Christ Jesus”? These individual experiences of God being for us will help us to have substance when we are together—particularly in the service of God, so that as in assembly we may reach glory to Him “in the assembly in Christ Jesus unto all generations of the age of ages”, Ephesians 3: 21. That is the very height of our approach to God, but to reach that depends, in measure, on whether we are able to resort to that area and have our mode of life patterned in relation to it. I feel that I can say very little about it, but I pass on these simple impressions that we all may be encouraged. The abstract is absolute; the experience is according to our measure. May our measure increase.
I desire, beloved brethren, to speak of our affections as related to the heavenly line of the truth. We have been speaking of how the Lord Jesus should have the right of way in our hearts and how

He builds inwards. The right of redemption would lie behind that, and it is very choice to think of the right which the Lord has to our hearts. So I think it is a question of the affections in a time of recovery that we have here in chapter 3 of the Song of Songs. We have had a high level of things up to this point in the book, but there has been departure and decline, so that at the opening of this chapter there is this expression, “On my bed, in the nights, I sought him”, as if it was a prolonged exercise, “I sought him whom my soul loveth”. We are all lovers of Jesus I trust, lovers of that blessed Man. What a privilege to be a lover of Christ!— to belong to that coming city—what a privilege! Now there is exercise here, suggesting that there has been a settling down in our circumstances, still having a desire after Christ but settling down lethargically, unresponsive to His heart. But He is not to be found in those circumstances of settling down; “I found Him not”.

Then she says, “I will rise now”. I think that this is the first movement towards recovery. Beloved brethren, we have passed through much; we have known low conditions—I just wish to bring it home to every heart as to where we have been. We can think of certain points in our history, “I sought him whom my soul loveth—I sought him, but I found him not”. Then the awakening—and there has definitely been an awakening in the souls of the saints. She sought him in the streets and broadways of the city. That was no place for a sister to be at that time. “The watchmen that go about the city found me”. She was in circumstances where perhaps her position would be questionable. Why was she there in the streets and broadways? There have been times in our experience when perhaps our position was questionable. I say it as understanding a little of these things through experience,

beloved brethren. “The watchmen that go about the city found me”; the Lord brings certain influences to bear upon us and we begin to consider where we are. There is a desire after Christ, a seeking after Him, but the way in which we are pursuing things is perhaps not altogether intelligent; but how gracious the Lord is, and He brings these influences to bear upon us to affect us.

Then I think there is a clear indication that she is affected, “Scarcely had I passed from them. When I found him whom my soul loveth”—beautiful language! Think of the grace of it! It is the grace of the dispensation. Has everyone here found the Lord Jesus? He has brought us through deep exercise with a view to getting deeper with us and touching our affections so that we arrive at a point like this, “I found him whom my soul loveth—I held him, and would not let him go”. This has been impressing my heart. What now comes to light is an energy of love that she had never known before. What has been our experience? Has the Lord reached this energy of love in your heart and in mine?

The days in which we are are finishing days, last days, difficult times, when we are surrounded by darkening influences. We need the energy of love. Well, have the experiences we have been through brought us to this, beloved brethren, “I held him”? It is very affecting, the point reached here. Are our hearts affected in relation to the heavenly line of the truth? It goes on to say, “I … brought him into my mother’s house. And into the chamber of her that conceived me”. What does this mean? I think it means that we know Jerusalem above which is our mother, a wonderful system of teaching under which we have been, the assembly. You must connect Him with the assembly. If you

think of Christ you must think of the assembly. Paul says, “I speak as to Christ, and as to the assembly” (Ephesians 5: 32), you must connect Him with the assembly, with the fellowship, with the circle where He is supreme. Think of the simplicity of this—yet the beauty of it.

When you come to Colossians, Paul gives us the wonderful glories of the Person of Christ. He presents Christ first, then he brings in the assembly. “He is head of the body, the assembly … firstborn from among the dead, that he might have the first place in all things”, Colossians 1: 13. The heavenly line of the truth is that you connect Him with the assembly. We have read, “If therefore ye have been raised with the Christ, seek the things which are above”. I think that the seeking indicates clearly that it is a question of the heart, “I sought him whom my soul loveth”. Our affections need to be seeking the things which are above, where He is.

I believe it connects with Colossians 2: 11, as to circumcision, the “putting off of the body of the flesh”; then it says, “buried with him in baptism”, and then it speaks of being raised with Him. I want to speak simply so that the youngest heart may be able to follow in some measure what I have to say. I think the truth is that we go out of sight. There is “the putting off of the body of the flesh in the circumcision of the Christ”; we go out of sight in baptism, and we reappear in resurrection, “raised with him through faith of the working of God”. It is a faith position, not yet resurrection in actuality, that is still to come, but it is a faith position taken in the power of the Spirit. We appear in that sense in life, for it goes on to speak of quickening, living in Christ’s life, living in relation to another order

of things altogether. Is that not beautiful, beloved brethren? It is the things above; it is not said to be the things in heaven. What scope there is as we begin to take it in. Let us seek the elevated things, the great heavenly line of the truth, things which are above, and have our hearts set in that relation, “Where the Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God”. Are we holding Him and not letting Him go? Are our hearts set in relation to this line of things, this wonderful heavenly line of the truth? We are in smallness—some localities are very small— but oh, beloved brethren, the truth is there. We are proving it, being set in relation to the greatest thoughts of divine love, the affections being in it.

Then it goes on to speak of the mind—“Have your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth”. This is a constant test. I think it means not at just some particular point, not occasionally, but constantly, our affections and our minds are to be set on the things above. There is so much to occupy our minds these days if we allow them to be influenced by it. The deterioration on every hand is so evident. Think of the moral deterioration and departure that is so evident. Think of the deterioration in government, the deterioration in industrial relations. All this is in contrast to setting our minds on things which are above. It takes us completely above. We have, of course, to move in this present scene. We have our part in responsibility, but in this line of things, by faith and the power of the Spirit, we can set our minds on this vast scope of the things that are above. I think it is essential to lovers of Christ, who are holding Him, that our minds and affections should be set along this line, so that we are living in relation to another order of things altogether, another Man and another world.

Well, it is a challenging thing for our hearts, beloved brethren, but how precious it is, and I suppose it would be right to say that we come into these experiences in the service of God. We take this ground by faith and in the power of the Spirit as buried with Christ and raised and quickened, ‘With Thee we died, in Thee we rise on high’, we sometimes sing. As the Lord comes in we take that ground of being with Him in life, and go on to the enjoyment of our highest assembly privileges. We all understand something of these precious things, that is one side, but I believe it is to be a constant matter that our affections are set on the things above where the Christ is sitting at the right hand of God, and that we set our minds on the things which are above and not on the things on the earth. It says, “for ye have died, and your life is hid with the Christ in God”.

When I read this passage it reminded me of a time, shortly after I came into fellowship, when an older brother said to me, ‘I was offered a ticket by a man I knew well for a concert on a certain night. I replied, Oh no, I am not interested in the concert. The man said to me, You people are just as good as dead; you do not go in for any of these things at all’. The brother said that it struck him quite forcibly—we are dead, and our life is hid with the Christ in God. People do not know where we are finding our life, and how precious it is to find it in relation to another order of things.

We need to consider the reality of the things which we enjoy, “Ye have died, and your life is hid with the Christ in God. When the Christ is manifested who is our life, then shall ye also be manifested with him in glory”. That is a scripture I love to think about. It brings the

transfiguration, as presented in Luke 9, to mind. Moses and Elias appeared with Him in glory. Think of the way in which those two men shone in the testimony. Moses the great minister, and Elijah who stood for the rights of God in a dark day. What men they were, and here they are appearing with Him in glory. Does it not stir our souls that we are going to be manifested with Him in glory? So what kind of persons should we be now? It ought to be a very affecting thing to us that we are going to be manifested with Him in glory, and I repeat, what kind of persons are we now? Are we going to be worthy? We can say from our hearts that these two men were worthy. Moses—the meekest man in all the earth, pointing on, as he does, to the Lord Jesus, the meek and lowly Man, but the feature was there in Moses—“very meek, above all men that were upon the face of the earth”, Numbers 12: 3. Think also of what shone out in Elijah as he sought to maintain the rights of God. Both these men appeared with Him in glory. Oh does it not affect our souls? When He who is our life shall be manifested, “then shall ye also be manifested with him in glory”. What an outlook for the older brothers and sisters especially, and what an outlook for the younger ones, too, the prospect of being manifested in glory with Jesus.

Now I wish to speak about the daughters of Zelophehad and what they sought. The children of Israel were nearing the time for going into the land, the culmination of the wilderness pathway, and these daughters of Zelophehad appear before Moses and Aaron, the princes, and the whole assembly. The position of these five daughters might suggest a certain weakness, and do we not feel the smallness of things? Sometimes this may affect us (I speak for myself), but let us not in any sense be discouraged. These five daughters of Zelophehad

represent true and intelligent assembly persons I would say. They are ready to speak of their father, he “died in the wilderness, and he was not in the band of them that banded themselves together against Jehovah in the band of Korah; but he died in his own sin … Why should the name of our father be taken away from his family?”. The desire of these sisters follows after the springing well in chapter 21, suggesting a true result of the service of the Holy Spirit in the hearts of the saints, a subjective result. They are going over and they are going to inherit.

Now God loves that. I say that because it is said clearly that the people “despised the pleasant land”, Psalm 106: 24. This is something that has been affecting me greatly. You know, beloved brethren, we want to think of our own position, as to where we are now, and perhaps it is easier than we think to despise the pleasant land and the great thoughts of God. Are we going the whole way? Colossians and Ephesians present the fulness of divine thoughts, the fulness of things relating to the assembly, thoughts of divine grace and love in all their beauty and fulness are brought out. Are we going the whole way? Do we appreciate what God has for us, the very best? Think of how the land is spoken of in Deuteronomy, as a land flowing with milk and honey. Think of its wealth. Are we on this line, or are we despising the pleasant land? It says, “See, brethren, lest there be in any one of you a wicked heart of unbelief” (Hebrews 3: 12), the affections affected adversely, despising the pleasant land.
Thank God we are still privileged, beloved brethren, for in the mercy of God we have been brought through. Think of the grace of our position that, although in weakness, all this lies

before us. The greatest thoughts of divine love lie before us. Are we going to appreciate them in our hearts? What an appreciation of heart there was in these sisters—“Give unto us a possession among the brethren of our father”. Dear young person, have you that desire, to inherit amongst the brethren?—for that is where you enjoy the great thoughts of divine love, in that circle where Jesus is loved, in which He is supreme. If you are holding Christ, you hold Him in relation to the assembly, and you hold Him in relation to the great thoughts of divine love. In Ephesians 1: 22 it says that God “gave him to be head over all things to the assembly, which is his body, the fulness of him who fills all in all”. Now that is a wonderful thing, what the assembly is as the body, representative of Christ. We know that in a coming day the assembly will be over the earth in relation to the universe (note how John speaks of the city and “her shining”). That is the idea of “the fulness of him who fills all in all”, but there is also the thought, I believe, of “the assembly which is his body”. If I might refer to Ephesians 3: 21, we have there the most wonderful things, “To him be glory in the assembly in Christ Jesus unto all generations of the age of ages”. The assembly is essential to the filling out of the service of God eternally.

Well, these are the things before us, beloved brethren; are we going to go the whole way? Moses presented their cause to Jehovah, and Jehovah said, “The daughters of Zelophehad speak right”. How pleasing to the blessed God when the hearts of the saints are set upon the inheritance! Do we say, ‘Give us the inheritance’? How good to look round on the brethren, however few, and to think of what is before us at this point in the testimony. Are we going the whole way? Are we set for the inheritance? God loves it to be so with His people.
Oh may our hearts delight the blessed God as they are filled with increased desire to go that way, to possess the inheritance. May it be so for His name’s sake.

articles.title: “THOU ART MY GOD”
articles.author: J. G. Chalmers
scriptures: Psalm 31: 3 (“Thou art my rock and fortress”), 4 (“Thou art my strength”), 14 (“Thou art my God”), 15 (“My times are in thy hand”)

paragraphs.text: The gospel is a great and glorious matter for in it God draws near to men in grace and love with the desire to gain men’s confidence and affections, and to effect in their souls the knowledge of Himself so that they might be happy and at home in His presence as there for the satisfaction of His love. We might think that God draws near to men just to forgive their sins. He does do that. If there is one present whose sins are not forgiven, we can tell you that God is near to you now and that He wants to forgive your sins. It is a fine thing to see a person troubled about his sins, in soul trouble. This psalm says, “Thou hast known the troubles of my soul” (Psalm 31: 7). You will find God near and ready and willing to forgive your sins. God’s present attitude to men is that of forgiveness. He is a forgiving God, and He has a perfectly righteous basis on which to forgive sins, the death of Christ, the One who has “once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God”, 1 Peter 3: 18. Thank God, there is efficacy in the blood of Jesus to cleanse the vilest sinners from their sins; “The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin”, 1 John 1: 7. If you are in trouble about your sins, then repent. God enjoins men to repent; “repentance towards God, and faith towards our Lord Jesus Christ”, Acts 20: 21. Then you will be blessed. God will fill you with all joy and peace in believing (Romans 15: 13).

But God has far more in mind for men even than that. He draws near to men in this scene where sin abounds—Oh the grace of it!—to disarm men of every wrong thought of Himself and to bring into their souls a substantial knowledge of Himself. God wants men to know Him, as Paul says, “I know whom I have believed”, 2 Timothy 1: 12. Can each one present say that? We are in a wonderful time. In Old Testament times God was but partially known. In Abraham’s day God was known as the Almighty God; in Israel’s day by the name of Jehovah; but when we come to the gospels it is God in Christ. God made known in a Man, “The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him”, John 1: 18. O, the Man of the gospels, Jesus! “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning to them their offences”, 2 Corinthians 5: 19. God is not charging men with their sins, He is forgiving them, justifying them, for He wants to gain their confidence and have them for the satisfaction of His love now and eternally. Christ has been here and He has made God known. He has suffered once for sins, He has died, He has been buried, and He has been raised again, raised by the glory of the Father. God is so satisfied with Christ and His work that He has raised Him and set Him down at His right hand in glory. That is the situation now. There is a Man in the glory, a wonderful sight! As the hymn says—
‘O the sight in heaven is glorious!
Man in righteousness is there’.

God is infinitely pleased with the Man Christ Jesus, the Man in righteousness in heaven, who has met His every claim against the sinner, and God is towards men in blessing in the glad tidings, declared by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven (1 Peter 1: 12). Oh what tidings these are! God wants men to know Him. Do you know God? He has been made known by a wonderful Name, the Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28: 19). Do you know the Father? Do you know the Son? Do you know the Holy Spirit? Have you a personal acquaintance with each divine Person? That is why I read in this Psalm, for David was a man who was rich in experience with God, and when he says, “Thou art my rock” it suggests a believer, in the light of christianity, speaking to Jesus for Scripture says, “the rock was the Christ”, 1 Corinthians 10: 4. When he says, “Thou art my strength” it suggests our speaking to the Holy Spirit, and when he says, “Thou art my God” it suggests our speaking to the Father, that is, as we approach this psalm in the light of the full revelation of God in the present economy.

Can each one say to Jesus, ‘Thou art my Rock’? ‘Oh’, you say, ‘I know Jesus as my Saviour, the One who has saved me from my sins, my Deliverer from the coming wrath’. Thank God for that! But can you say to Jesus, ‘Thou art my Rock’? It means that you are conscious by the Spirit of a living link in faith and affection with the Man in the glory. We need to appreciate Christ as the Rock, the One who was smitten of God ere the blessing could come to us. God smote His well beloved Son. How touching! God felt doing that; Jesus felt it too; but Jesus is now risen and glorified and He
is the Rock to be spoken to.

Do you ever speak to Jesus as the Rock? If you have a sense of need in your soul, speak to Jesus and you will find the waters flowing to fill and satisfy you. “If any one thirst, let him come to me and drink”, John 7: 37. The Spirit is available to be drunk into since Christ has been smitten and glorified; the waters are flowing. Then you will remember that when Moses asked God to see His glory God said, “Behold, there is a place by me—there shalt thou stand on the rock”, Exodus 33: 21. Have we the desire to see the glory of God? It is to be seen; it shines in the face of Jesus, and we can contemplate it there. It is vast. This is something to be reached in our souls, to be conscious that God has put us in Christ, and there is no condemnation to those in Christ Jesus (Romans 8: 1). Christ is alive, the Man in the glory, the centre of God’s world, and we are in Him; that is our place, near to God, “a place by me … on the rock”. What favour! Nothing can shake a person who has a living link in affection with the Man in the glory, the Rock. Such a person is on solid ground, he can say, ‘On Christ the solid Rock I stand’; he can say appreciatively, “Thou art my rock”. Then He is our fortress. Do not be ashamed to confess Jesus as Lord. His name is a strong tower, the righteous runneth into it and is safe (Proverbs 18: 10). It is a fortress, impregnable, unassailable, unshakable.

Then David says, “Thou art my strength”. The Holy Spirit is our strength. He is the One who gives us power for spiritual things. We come to that experimentally in Romans 8. Romans 7 is the struggle of a believer. It is good to see a person in that struggle for it shows that he is exercised to get on spiritually. You want to do what is

right and you feel powerless to do it. What you learn is that the flesh in you does not change when you are converted, when you become a believer. It is still the same flesh as in your unconverted days, and God expects nothing good from it. He has condemned sin in the flesh. In the struggle you feel the need of deliverance, and the Deliverer is Christ; you turn away from yourself to Christ, the Man in the glory. Then you learn to appreciate the Spirit. He is available from God’s side on the principle of gift, the gift of God. God gives the Holy Spirit to those that obey Him (Acts 5: 32). Our side is to receive the Spirit. The Lord Jesus says that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to them that ask Him (Luke 11: 13). It is only in the power of the Spirit that we can overcome the flesh. “If, by the Spirit, ye put to death the deeds of the body, ye shall live”, Romans 8: 13. When you thus get the victory you do not take the credit but you thank the Spirit, you say in affection, “Thou art my strength”. You fulfil righteousness in the power of the Spirit. These are real experiences.

Then the Spirit is the earnest of the inheritance (Ephesians 1: 13). He gives us the present joy amongst the saints of our eternal portion. He empowers us to answer feelingly to Christ as His brethren and as His assembly, His bride. As the Spirit of God’s Son in our hearts He empowers us to answer to the Father in the feelings, affections, and intelligence proper to sonship. As the Father’s Spirit He strengthens us with power in the inner man fully to apprehend with all the saints the vast scene of glory that subsists for the pleasure of God and to render to God glory in the assembly in Christ Jesus. All this should cause us to say to the Spirit, “Thou art my strength”. Do you really know the Spirit as conscious of His indwelling you? The Lord Jesus said, “Ye know him, for he abides with

you, and shall be in you”, John 14: 17. There is no affinity between the world and the Spirit. A sister local here once said in conversation, ‘We would not have one thought Godward apart from the Spirit’. The Spirit helps us to know a vast range of things, the things which have been freely given to us of God (1 Corinthians 2: 12). In the appreciation of this we can say in affection, “Thou art my strength”.

Then David says, “Thou art my God”. Paul says, “To us there is one God, the Father”, 1 Corinthians 8: 6. Can you say, ‘My God and Father’? The believer belongs to the most dignified family in the universe, the family of God. “As many as received him, to them gave he the right to be children of God” (John 1: 12), also “See what love the Father has given to us, that we should be called the children of God”, 1 John 3: 1. The believer can say now, “Thou art my God” in the sense of this family relationship. He can say it, too, in the testimonial sphere, as in the path of separation in faithfulness to Christ, where he proves the Father in a circumstantial way; “I will be to you for a Father, and ye shall be to me for sons and daughters”, 2 Corinthians 6: 18. What an advantage the believer has over the man in the world! He has God as his Father, and he can say, in circumstances however testing, “Thou art my God”. But there is something even greater. God has marked us out for sonship through Jesus Christ to Himself; that is His purpose. In the assembly, in the service of God, we know God in His own realm of purpose and we trace every blessing to Him, the glorious source of all. There we can say happily, freely, and thankfully, “Thou art my God”.
Then David says, “My times are in thy hand”. What a touch that is! We think of the times the saints in this place are going through, the sorrow on our spirits in regard to our sister who is so

ill, and the saints in Macduff, where only this afternoon the Lord took a sister to Himself; but we can say restfully that our times are in His hand. The Lord Jesus says that times are in the Father’s authority (Acts 1: 7). God thought of you in purpose and your times are in His hand, as the hymn says, ‘Whatever they may be, pleasing or painful, dark or bright, as best may seem to Thee’—the same God. We wonder at times why some have so much discipline, so much sorrow, so much bereavement, so much testing, yet one who really knows God can say, “My times are in thy hand”, and they could not be in better hands, for the Father’s hand will never cause His child a needless tear! The sorrows, bereavements, and pressure are testing us all as to our knowledge of God. Do we really know Him? David had many testings, far more than we may have thought of, for the Psalms are the fruit of his actual experiences. Scripture speaks of the times that passed over David (1 Chronicles 29: 30) but he can say, “My times are in thy hand”.

Paul would say the same, even though in prison at Philippi or Rome (What choice epistles came from him in that Roman prison!)—he knew his God and that his times were in His hand. Oh I trust that each of us will grow in the knowledge of God so as to be able to say to Jesus, “Thou art my rock”, and to the Spirit, “Thou art my strength”, and to the Father, “Thou art my God”, and to say, in the restfulness of spirit that becomes persons who know their God, “My times are in thy hand”. May it be so, for His name’s sake.

INFLUENCE A remark was made, recently as to the influence which each of us has on others. It reminded one of an interesting illustration in the solar system. About 1840 astronomers found that the planet Uranus, discovered some sixty years earlier, was at times moving faster, and at times more slowly, than calculations based on known factors had predicted. It was then realised that an unknown, more distant, planet was influencing Uranus by its power of attraction. This led to the position of the “new” planet (now known as Neptune) being calculated, and then to its being located in the heavens. Now each of us, from morning to night, has some influence on every person we meet. Is it a christian influence? As to my fellow christians, does it encourage them in the direction of what is spiritual?—or does it tend to attract them to what is earthly or worldly? Is Christ, in some measure, in expression? or is it the ugliness of the flesh? Let us be deeply concerned that our influence is a right one. Let us ask the Lord to help us to be an influence for Him, a saving influence in a world where the whole pull is in the wrong direction.
